analysis.one_liner: Adds up to 20 hours a week of home care help to Medicare for older adults and people with disabilities.
analysis.headline: The Medicare at Home Act was introduced with zero cosponsors in August 2026 and never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare today pays for hospital care, doctor visits, and short-term home health, but not for long-term help with everyday tasks like bathing, dressing, and eating. This bill would add a home care benefit covering up to 20 hours a week of a home care worker's time for Medicare beneficiaries who need help with at least two daily activities. The added cost would be financed through Medicare Part B premiums, with an official estimate of the premium impact due within 180 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need hands-on help with daily living — more than 10 million people by the bill's own findings — plus the family members who currently fill the gap with unpaid care. The bill says out-of-pocket home care can cost more than $60,000 a year, costs this benefit would replace, and that unpaid family caregivers already provide over $1 trillion in unpaid care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled Medicare beneficiaries; family caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would cover up to 20 hours per week of help with activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, eating) and instrumental activities (meals, medication reminders, related housekeeping) delivered in the beneficiary's home. [S2]

Eligibility requires only Medicare enrollment plus a care plan certifying need for help with at least two daily activities — no asset test, no spend-down into Medicaid as Medicare currently requires for long-term care. [S2]

The bill's findings cite out-of-pocket home care costs exceeding $60,000 annually, and say the benefit would relieve unpaid family caregivers who provide over $1 trillion in unpaid care to the economy. [S2]
The payment methodology must reflect a reasonable wage floor for home care workers, meaning the new federal funding is required to support worker pay. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries, through higher monthly Part B premiums adjusted to the benefit's actuarial cost (though lower-income beneficiaries get the standard premium subsidy), and federal taxpayers, who fund roughly three-quarters of Part B costs through general revenue. The benefit also adds a permanent entitlement to Medicare's long-term obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare beneficiaries via premiums, plus taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill is financed by raising Part B premiums, so beneficiaries themselves would pay a substantial share of the new benefit's cost, and the bill leaves the actual premium impact to an actuarial report rather than fixing it. [S2]

The 20-hour weekly cap covers only part of the need for people with heavy care requirements, and the bill excludes anyone already receiving duplicative long-term care through Medicaid, so it supplements rather than replaces the existing system. [S2]

The benefit does not start until more than two years after enactment, and the Secretary must first write rules on worker qualifications and agency enrollment, so real-world help would be years away. [S2]

A good-faith objection: a new open-ended home care entitlement funded by premiums and federal revenue is expensive and permanent, and critics of Medicare expansion argue the cost and fraud-control burden deserves fuller analysis than a single actuarial report.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit addresses a real and widely supported gap — most people believe Medicare already covers long-term home care, and it does not — and it replaces costs that families currently absorb privately or by impoverishing themselves into Medicaid. The honest costs are real: higher premiums for all Part B enrollees, permanent federal spending, and a benefit that helps most but not all of the people who need care. The design is modest and capped rather than open-ended, but the financing was left deliberately vague, which would have been a major point of negotiation had the bill advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2026 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote as the 119th Congress runs out of time.

narrative.text: Sen. Andy Kim introduced the Medicare at Home Act on August 5, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance. [S4]
The bill had zero cosponsors as of the provided record. [S3]
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in its action history. [S4]
The bill's own findings cite polling that 93 percent of adults agree Medicare should cover home care, and that large majorities of current beneficiaries wrongly believe it already does. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to pay for the new benefit and the home care industry has not gained a new federal revenue stream — but the more than 10 million Medicare beneficiaries needing help with daily living are no closer to coverage, and family caregivers keep filling the gap unpaid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: beneficiaries uncovered, no new costs

for.name: Sen. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare at Home Act and became its only sponsor; no other senator signed on. [S1]

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the record. [S4]

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor time, consistent with the bill's absence from any floor calendar or vote in the action history. [S4]

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes, so no partisan pattern was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and home care workers
industries.note: The bill creates a new federal customer base by making millions of Medicare beneficiaries eligible for publicly paid home care, routed through agencies and individual workers enrolled in Medicare. Its payment rules require a wage floor, so industry revenue and worker pay would rise together with the benefit.

Because the benefit is added to Part B, Medicare Advantage plans would be required to cover it, adding plan costs; the bill does not detail how plans would be paid for it, leaving the effect ambiguous.

Currently, families spend down their savings into Medicaid to get long-term care, which states partly fund. A Medicare benefit that avoids duplicating Medicaid services would shift some of that demand off state budgets onto Medicare.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and no committee action with only weeks left in the 119th Congress. Bills in this position almost never reach a floor vote; the most likely outcome is that it dies when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless reintroduced in the next Congress.
